title: Consistent Hash Ring
description: Map keys to servers with a hash ring and virtual nodes so that few keys move when servers change.
statement:
Build `HashRing(nodes=(), replicas=100)`, which maps keys to servers (nodes) so that adding or removing a node moves only a small share of the keys.

Each node sits on a circle at `replicas` positions (its virtual nodes), each position being the hash of the node's name plus the replica number. `node_for(key)` hashes the key onto the circle and returns the node at the first position after it, going clockwise and wrapping around from the end.

- `add(node)` puts a node on the ring (adding one that is already there changes nothing). `remove(node)` takes it off (removing one that is not there changes nothing).
- `node_for` returns `None` for an empty ring. Nodes and keys are strings.
- Hash with `hashlib.md5`, not `hash()`: Python's string hash changes every time the interpreter starts, so keys would move after a restart.
- A node's positions depend only on its own name, never on the other nodes or on the order they were added in.

**Example**

```python
ring = HashRing(["cache-1", "cache-2", "cache-3"])
ring.node_for("user:42")   # one of the three nodes, always the same for this key
ring.remove("cache-2")     # only the keys that lived on cache-2 move; every other key stays put
```

tests.name: an empty ring has no owner for a key
with one node, that node owns every key
a key always goes to the same node, whatever order the nodes were added in
tests.code:
first = HashRing(["a", "b", "c"])
second = HashRing(["c", "a", "b"])
third = HashRing()
for node in ["b", "c", "a"]:
    third.add(node)
assert difference(placement(first), placement(second)) == None
assert difference(placement(first), placement(third)) == None

tests.name: virtual nodes even out the load: with 10 nodes each owns between 5% and 16% of 5,000 keys
removing a node moves only the keys that were on it
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(["a", "b", "c", "d"])
before = placement(ring)
ring.remove("c")
after = placement(ring)
assert [key for key in KEYS if before[key] != "c" and before[key] != after[key]] == []
assert "c" not in set(after.values()), "keys are still being sent to the removed node"

tests.name: adding a node only takes keys from the others, and about a quarter of them for a 4th node
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(["a", "b", "c"])
before = placement(ring)
ring.add("d")
after = placement(ring)
moved = [key for key in KEYS if before[key] != after[key]]
assert [key for key in moved if after[key] != "d"] == []
assert 0.10 < len(moved) / len(KEYS) < 0.40, f"{len(moved) / len(KEYS):.0%} of the keys moved; about a quarter should"

tests.name: adding a node and removing it again puts every key back
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(["a", "b", "c"])
before = placement(ring)
ring.add("d")
ring.remove("d")
assert difference(before, placement(ring)) == None

tests.name: no key falls off the end of the ring (try one position per node)
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(["a", "b", "c"], replicas=1)
owners = set(placement(ring).values())
assert owners <= {"a", "b", "c"}, f"keys were sent to {owners - {'a', 'b', 'c'}}, which is not a node"

tests.name: adding a node twice is the same as adding it once
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(["a", "b"])
ring.add("b")
ring.add("b")
ring.remove("b")
assert set(placement(ring).values()) == {"a"}

tests.name: removing an unknown node changes nothing; removing the last node empties the ring
tests.code:
ring = HashRing(["a", "b"])
before = placement(ring)
ring.remove("zzz")
assert difference(before, placement(ring)) == None
ring.remove("a")
ring.remove("b")
assert ring.node_for("user:1") == None

hints: Picture the range of hash values bent into a circle. Where would you put the servers, where does a key land, and which server owns it? What keeps the lookup fast?

Keep the positions (the hash of `node#replica`) in a sorted list, with a dict from position to node. For a key, binary-search (`bisect`) the first position after its hash, and wrap around to the start when you run off the end.

Use `% len(positions)` for the wrap-around, and make adding an existing node and removing an unknown one do nothing, or duplicate positions and ghosts of removed nodes stay behind. Hash with md5: `hash()` of a string differs in every run.
explanation:
**The problem with `hash(key) % n`.** Going from `n` to `n + 1` servers changes the answer for almost every key, so nearly the whole cache is invalidated at once.

**The ring.** Hash each server onto a circle (here the integers up to 2¹²⁸, wrapping around). A key belongs to the first server clockwise from the key's own hash. A new server now takes over only the keys between it and its predecessor (about 1/n of them), and a removed server hands its keys to the next one clockwise; nothing else moves.

**Virtual nodes.** With one point per server the arcs are very uneven, so one server can own several times more keys than another. Placing each server at many points (`replicas`) averages that out, and it also spreads a removed server's keys across all the others instead of dumping them on one neighbour.

**Implementation.** A sorted list of positions and a dict from position to node: a lookup is a binary search (`bisect`) followed by `% len(positions)` to wrap around. Positions come only from the node's name and the replica number, which is what makes "only the changed node's keys move" true. Hash with `hashlib.md5`; the built-in `hash()` of a string is randomised in every process.

**Complexity.** Lookup is O(log(nodes × replicas)). Adding or removing a node costs the hashing of its `replicas` positions plus a re-sort here; a balanced tree would avoid the re-sort. Distributed caches, sharded databases and load balancers use this idea.
